title: You Can't Trust Your AI Bill. And Neither Can I
gist: CloudZero founder Erik Peterson argues AI spend will eclipse cloud bills, citing per-token costs down while enterprise spend rises 222% (Jevons Paradox) and a 14x rise in GenAI spend over five months at CloudZero. He says AI bills are opaque and unreliable, tokenmaxxing is wasteful, and teams should govern spend with unit economics, spend limits and margin-based model routing ahead of a predicted autonomous cloud by 2028.

insights.claim: AI vendor bills are as opaque as a utility bill (a million tokens for a dollar amount) with no itemization of what is behind the spend, so even CloudZero's founder says he cannot fully trust AI billing data.
insights.speaker: Erik Peterson
insights.so_what: Buyers lack cost transparency, creating demand for AI cost attribution and FinOps tooling.
insights.quote: I built a company that built the category, and I can't actually fully trust our bill either.
insights.locator: Act 1: The Confession

insights.claim: University of Maryland researchers developed CoIn, 'the cost of the invisible', to measure large hidden spend behind AI usage that is not shown on the bill.
insights.speaker: Erik Peterson
insights.so_what: Evidence that invisible token consumption is material and being studied academically.
insights.quote: They call it CoIn, the cost of the invisible.
insights.locator: Nobody agrees on the unit

insights.claim: AI vendors have no common billing unit: formulas differ for code, images and audio, some charge for silence, and schemas and terms vary, which makes consolidated cost data hard to build.
insights.speaker: Erik Peterson
insights.so_what: Lack of a standard unit complicates cross-vendor cost comparison and favors normalization layers.
insights.quote: Nobody agrees on the unit.
insights.locator: Nobody agrees on the unit

insights.claim: Pricing is incoherent: o1 remains available at 7.5 times the cost of vastly superior models, region choice can raise prices, and a tokenizer change can raise token costs by 35% without any change under the customer's control.
insights.speaker: Erik Peterson
insights.so_what: Hidden price shifts make AI budgets unpredictable.
insights.quote: They change how they tokenize things. Token costs go up 35%.
insights.locator: The prices themselves also don't make any sense.

insights.claim: Billing APIs from AI providers are unreliable, with daily 500 errors in the last 90 days, and Anthropic Enterprise billing data had no proper API until March.
insights.speaker: Erik Peterson
insights.so_what: Immature billing infrastructure is a gap for tooling vendors.
insights.quote: We didn't even have a proper API to pull Anthropic Enterprise billing data down, until March.
insights.locator: It's happening everywhere.

insights.claim: Tokenmaxxing, treating AI token consumption as a performance leaderboard, is called possibly the most expensive vanity metric in IT history, estimated at $5 billion to $15 billion.
insights.speaker: Erik Peterson
insights.so_what: Token spend as a status metric inflates vendor revenue and corporate waste at once.
insights.quote: This is single-handedly probably the most expensive vanity metric in the history of IT.
insights.locator: We are here. Really, we are here.

insights.claim: Engineers who fear being fired stay silent as hundreds of thousands of dollars go out over a weekend, because management signaled that high spend is good; budget alerts and dashboards are ignored.
insights.speaker: Erik Peterson
insights.so_what: Alerts cannot help if culture discourages raising them; hard limits are needed.
insights.quote: Every company that we've looked at, they had plenty of dashboards.
insights.locator: Every company that we've looked at, they had plenty of dashboards.

insights.claim: There are no per-call or per-user spend limits on AI tools, and if every engineer can spend $5,000 in 12 hours, a company can exhaust its capital in a couple of weeks.
insights.speaker: Erik Peterson
insights.so_what: Spend governance and hard caps become a product category and risk-control item.
insights.quote: It's very easy for any company of any size to spend the total of its capital in a couple of weeks if they let this thing go.
insights.locator: It's very easy for any company of any size

insights.claim: The author predicts Denial-of-Wallet attacks in which an attacker with access to a company's AWS environment uses Bedrock tokens, billing the victim, will put some companies out of business.
insights.speaker: Erik Peterson
insights.so_what: AI token spend is a new attack surface; security teams should cap and monitor model access.
insights.quote: Denial-of-Wallet is coming.
insights.locator: Security is not to be forgotten either.

insights.claim: Companies including Uber and JPMorgan overspent on AI, Microsoft told staff to stop using Claude, and Uber's CEO asked what connects the spending to outcomes; one reported spending about $40 million in a quarter against a $4 million annual plan.
insights.speaker: Erik Peterson
insights.so_what: Enterprise AI budgets are overrunning plans, which will force ROI scrutiny.
insights.quote: Microsoft just literally days ago said, stop using Claude.
insights.locator: What's the aftermath of all this?

insights.claim: Spend per engineer varies widely with similar outcomes, driven by how context windows are packed, planning discipline and MCP overhead, with runaway loops spending money for days.
insights.speaker: Erik Peterson
insights.so_what: Efficiency of AI usage differs between users, so training and tooling matter for cost.
insights.quote: Wildly different spend, similar outcomes.
insights.locator: There was just days ago, again, another thing

themes.theme: Jevons paradox and the cost to build

insights.claim: The author claims AI will eclipse the cloud bill and that all cloud spend will be absorbed by AI, with current cloud growth being only a warm-up.
insights.speaker: Erik Peterson
insights.so_what: Positions AI inference and agent spend as the main growth driver of infrastructure budgets.
insights.quote: I believe all cloud spend is going to be absorbed by AI.
insights.locator: Act 2: The Eclipse

insights.claim: Token cost per unit is down about 1000% while enterprise AI spend is up 222%, an example of Jevons Paradox in which greater efficiency increases total consumption.
insights.speaker: Erik Peterson
insights.so_what: Falling token prices will not reduce budgets; expect volume growth to dominate.
insights.quote: Cost per tokens are down by 1000% but our enterprise spend is up by 222%.
insights.locator: Act 3: The Inversion

insights.claim: CloudZero sees GenAI spend grow fourteen times in five months, about 80% of it overhead from requests, systems, R&D, humans and Claude Code, and one customer's spend went from 0 to 2 million in a month after a new model appeared.
insights.speaker: Erik Peterson
insights.so_what: Provides a vendor-observed data point on how quickly enterprise AI spend scales on new models.
insights.quote: Fourteen times growth in GenAI spend in the last five months.
insights.locator: Act 3: The Inversion

insights.claim: For some CFOs the cost to build now exceeds the cost to serve, and they compare employee pay to token cost in spreadsheets.
insights.speaker: Erik Peterson
insights.so_what: The AI cost conversation has moved from engineering FinOps to the CFO P&L, raising scrutiny of headcount versus tokens.
insights.quote: The inversion is this magical thing that some CFOs have started to notice which is the cost to build is now the most expensive thing, not the cost to serve.
insights.locator: Act 3: The Inversion

insights.claim: Less than 2% of users pick cheaper models, as most rush to the newest model even though models are different tools for different tasks rather than strict upgrades.
insights.speaker: Erik Peterson
insights.so_what: Model routing to cheaper models is a large untapped savings lever.
insights.quote: Then, who's using the cheaper models? Less than 2% of you.
insights.locator: Act 3: The Inversion

insights.claim: Every AI startup combined is still eight times short of the total AI CapEx spend of the cloud providers, leaving a large funding gap.
insights.speaker: Erik Peterson
insights.so_what: The gap raises questions about who ultimately finances AI capex.
insights.quote: every AI startup combined is still eight times short of the total AI CapEx spend of all the cloud providers
insights.locator: Act 2: The Eclipse

insights.claim: Anthropic claims a 5% profit return while OpenAI shows negative 122%, both with roughly 80% margins on API calls, making the AI supply chain potentially the most profitable in tech while the funding circle keeps spinning.
insights.speaker: Erik Peterson
insights.so_what: API gross margins are high but corporate profitability differs widely and depends on continued capital circulation.
insights.quote: OpenAI has got a negative 122%.
insights.locator: They're both burning cash if we look at both of the giants out there.

insights.claim: The author predicts a fully autonomous cloud in which AI writes, deploys and manages code, with the cloud as we know it done by 2028.
insights.speaker: Erik Peterson
insights.so_what: Aggressive timeline; implies infrastructure purchasing and operations shifting to machine-driven decisions.
insights.quote: My bet is that it's all done and figured out by 2028.
insights.locator: Act 1

insights.claim: By 2027 the primary buyer of technology and cloud resources will be an autonomous AI system, causing cost to build and cost to serve to track together on a steeper curve.
insights.speaker: Erik Peterson
insights.so_what: Machine buyers need machine-readable cost signals and governance.
insights.quote: The primary buyer of things, technology, cloud resources, stuff in your environment is not going to be humans, it's going to be an autonomous AI system.
insights.locator: Key Takeaway

insights.claim: AI is giving engineers a forced promotion from doing the work to managing the work, and the author no longer looks at the code, caring only about tests and validation of outcomes.
insights.speaker: Erik Peterson
insights.so_what: Engineering value shifts toward judgement, specification and verification.
insights.quote: I got a confession to make, I don't look at the code anymore.
insights.locator: I have given up on that dream.

insights.claim: The author expects LLM-produced code to converge on whatever language is most efficient for LLMs rather than human-readable languages.
insights.speaker: Erik Peterson
insights.so_what: Speculative; would shift language and tooling ecosystems.
insights.quote: All code that is produced will eventually be whatever the LLMs can produce in the most efficient manner possible.
insights.locator: I have given up on that dream.

insights.claim: Every decision is now a buying decision: everyday searches once free on Google now go through paid LLMs like Perplexity, Claude and ChatGPT, raising questions about what counts as waste against the roughly 30% cloud waste baseline.
insights.speaker: Erik Peterson
insights.so_what: Consumption of paid inference replaces free search, expanding AI revenue pools.
insights.quote: Every decision is now a buying decision.
insights.locator: Act 5: Think Different

themes.theme: Governing AI spend with unit economics

insights.claim: Measure unit economics, the cost of the thing your product does, rather than cost per token, because optimizing a proxy metric invites Goodhart's Law and a bare token bill does not show what feature or outcome it drove.
insights.speaker: Erik Peterson
insights.so_what: Companies that can attribute AI cost to features and customers can defend margins.
insights.quote: If we measure cost per token, your team is going to optimize for cost per token.
insights.locator: We got to also measure the right things.

insights.claim: Route models by margin and customer value, so that top-tier customers, free tiers and high-margin tiers do not all use the same expensive model.
insights.speaker: Erik Peterson
insights.so_what: Margin-aware routing is a direct gross-margin lever for AI-enabled software.
insights.quote: Route according to margin or your profit objective.
insights.locator: What's going to be the margin yield

insights.claim: Dashboards are post-mortems; the primary users of cost systems will be AI agents that prefer JSON, so real-time machine-readable cost data should replace dashboards, and CFOs are starting to ask for real-time data.
insights.speaker: Erik Peterson
insights.so_what: Opportunity for real-time cost APIs and automated enforcement over visualization.
insights.quote: Dashboards are just post-mortems of a horrible event that occurred
insights.locator: Stop Doing This on Monday - Five Defaults

insights.claim: Engineers should express efficiency gains in business terms, such as cost per transaction falling from 25 cents to 10 cents, since finance leaders respond to unit costs rather than technology names like Kubernetes.
insights.speaker: Erik Peterson
insights.so_what: Framing engineering projects in unit-cost terms wins budget approval.
insights.quote: It costs us 25 cents per transaction. It's going to go to 10 cents per transaction.
insights.locator: Participant 2

insights.claim: Rolling out Claude Code and co-work to all 180 employees at CloudZero turned everyone, including the head of HR, into a junior developer, and then 'everything blew up'.
insights.speaker: Erik Peterson
insights.so_what: Democratized coding increases shadow software and governance load on IT.
insights.quote: everybody in the company became a developer, a very junior developer, in that moment
insights.locator: The CIO and the CFO seem to be having a moment.

insights.claim: The cost of knowledge is approaching zero while the cost of wisdom will approach infinity; economics may be more valuable to study than computer science.
insights.speaker: Erik Peterson
insights.so_what: Judgement and cost literacy become scarce skills.
insights.quote: The cost of knowledge is rapidly approaching zero, but the cost of wisdom is going to go near infinite.
insights.locator: Education, that's a whole other conversation.
